hypotheses.justification: The statement holds for every real h. The key fact is that |min 1 x| ≤ |x| for every real x: if x ≥ 1 then min 1 x = 1 ≤ x, and if x < 1 then min 1 x = x. So ‖min 1 (a s / h) * min 1 (b s / h)‖ ≤ |a s / h| * |b s / h| = |a s * b s| / (h*h). This also covers h = 0, where Lean's convention a/0 = 0 makes both sides 0. Since |a s * b s| ≤ a s^2 + b s^2, the norm is bounded by (a s^2 + b s^2)/(h*h). That bound is summable by `(ha2.add hb2).div_const (h*h)`, which is how `LengthArea.summable_mul_of_squares` itself is proved. `Summable.of_norm_bounded` then finishes. No step uses 0 < h. Each of hh, ha and hb can be deleted on its own, and all three can also be deleted together.

The proof uses ha only to show that the min factors are nonnegative, so that the absolute value can be dropped. A sign-free argument works instead. For any real x, |min 1 x| ≤ |x| (if x ≥ 1 the min is 1 ≤ x, otherwise the min is x). Hence ‖min 1 (a s/h) * min 1 (b s/h)‖ ≤ |a s|*|b s|/(h*h) ≤ (a s^2 + b s^2)/(h*h). The right side is summable by `(ha2.add hb2).div_const (h*h)`, and `Summable.of_norm_bounded` concludes. The case h = 0 is trivial because x/0 = 0. Negative values of a s are therefore harmless. Each of hh, ha and hb can be deleted on its own, and all three together.

This is the same as for ha, by symmetry. The bound |min 1 x| ≤ |x| holds for every real x, so the norm of the term is at most |a s|*|b s|/(h*h) ≤ (a s^2 + b s^2)/(h*h). That is summable by `(ha2.add hb2).div_const (h*h)`, and `Summable.of_norm_bounded` gives the result without any sign condition on b. The case h = 0 is trivial because x/0 = 0. Each of hh, ha and hb can be deleted on its own, and all three together.
